content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a persistent homology (PH) based contrastive learning GCN network for time series forecasting with graph. The key contribution is on PH-based graph generation and representation, but it was not justified and explained well. Also the paper claims efficiency and extracts more "hidden information". I did not see any experiment results about it.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: Time series forecasting with a graph is an important problem. 

Weakness: 
1. The paper is not self-contained and did not explain PH in great detail.
2. The writing quality is unnecessarily complicated and the notation is very difficult to read. 
3. The explanation on persistent-based data augmentation is not sufficient. 
4. No experiments demonstrated any benefit of persistent-based augmentation, except some performance improved marginally.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is not clear at all and the writing quality needs significant improvement. Since the core concept of PH is not well explained in an intuitive way, the novelty is difficult to evaluate.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This work proposes a persistent homology (PH) based contrastive learning GCN network for time series forecasting with graph. I have several problems with the paper. 

1. The key novel and the contribution is on PH-based graph generation and representation, however, the authors failed to explain the idea and why it is important. For example, what pattern family does the graph look like visually? What do you mean by shape of graph? Any examples? How large is each PH family and how many nodes do PH consists?
2. The writing is very hard to follow. The entire section 3.2 looks like a GCN but it is written in a very messy and complex way. PD was not touched after section 3.3. How is it related and used in the algorithms? 
3. Figure 1 after reading Appx B is still a mystery. The presentation and notation are very confusing. 
4. Figure 2. I am totally lost. 
5. In the experiment, it seems PCL-GCRN is only better in performance. The authors claim the key benefit of using topological graph contrastive learning is on "hidden information" and "less computation costs" at the top of page 7. But there is no experiment to show that. 

I am afraid there are too many unclear parts and the paper is not presented in a way for easy comprehension. My recommendation is a rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new architecture for graph analysis for forecasting time series. The proposed method combines graph convolution-based recurrent network and contrastive learning using TDA-based data augmentation. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, ablation studies are being conducted to compare the performance of the proposed method with conventional methods and to verify the effectiveness of each function.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The concept of each function is known, but they are built to be effective for the specific desired data/tasks.
- Especially since there is no clearly effective method for graph pertubation, so it would be interesting to achieve this on a TDA basis.
- It has also been compared to many conventional methods and shown to be more effective than them.

Weakness
- My biggest concern is the assurance against perturbing the persistent diagram instead of the perturbation of the graph as far as S1-S7 in P6 is concerned. That is, does the graph corresponding to the perturbed PD exist, and if so, does the corresponding graph have the same characteristics in terms of the task we want to analyze as it did before the perturbation? This is a prerequisite for contrastive learning, but does not generally hold true for graphs. I imagine they are not a problem for graph data intended for time series forecasting, but they may limit the types of perturbations. Also, it seems to me that the perturbation of the PD and the perturbation of the graph can be mapped to some extent for this task, but if that is the case, there is no need to discuss it in the PD and we can do the contrastive learning with the graph as it is. It would be better to show the value of doing this in PD.
- As it relates to the above concern, the method of perturbation of PD should be more specifically described.
- In the Table1-3 experiment, why are there different methods of comparison for different data sets? It seems to me that you are hiding something inconvenient. If there are appropriate reasons that cannot be stated, such as inability to reproduce, please write them down.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Although heuristic, it is basically clearly stated and well validated by experimentation. The assignment and idea are sufficiently novel and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: As a method of graph analysis for time series forecasting, we propose an architecture that improves performance and show its effectiveness in experiments. Implicitly, the characteristics of the time-series forecasting task seem to circumvent the concerns of the method, but if the proposal is a method for time-series forecasting, the problem is not serious.However, it is advisable to have a discussion on these matters. Also, the method of perturbation lacks specificity, so I would like to see a more specific description.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work devises a topological-invariance-based data augmentation approach devoted to contrastive graph learning for multivariate time-series forecasting. Experiments on 6 real-world datasets validate the proposed PCL-GCRN outperforms existing RNN-, CNN-, and GNN-based baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros. 

This work emphasizes the concept of topological invariance in spatiotemporal data for the time-series forecasting task.

Cons.
1. The technical contributions of this work are mainly incremental, which makes this work not technically sound. The data augmentation adopted by the authors can hardly be taken as a novel technique for contrastive graph learning or spatiotemporal prediction tasks. 
2. The presentation of this work is problematic. Typos and grammar errors exist throughout this draft. Besides, the methodology part is not well organized, such that the logic is not fluent and easy to follow. 
3. Existing SOTA multivariate time-series algorithms are Transformer-based, such as Autoformer, Informer, etc., which are not compared in the experiments. 
4. More elaborated performance comparisons should be conducted. For example, the prediction performance w.r.t. varying input and output lengths.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
>> Clarity 

The presentation of this work is not well-organized. Many long paragraphs and sentences are encountered in the methodology part. 

>> Novelty

This work lacks novelty in terms of technical contribution to the communities of contrastive learning and time-series forecasting. 

>> Reproducibility

Though the experimental settings are provided, the reproducibility statement is missing.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors in this work put efforts to address the multivariate time-series forecasting on top of spatiotemporal data modeling. They focus on the concept of persistent homology and exploit this topological invariance property of data to develop the data augmentation approach for contrastive graph learning, which can benefit the future prediction for spatiotemporal predictive applications. 

However, the claimed contributions of this work are incremental and not significant. One can not say that devising data augmentation methods with existing perturbing techniques is technically novel for the contrastive learning community. 
Besides, the experiments of this work are not convincing. Not only the important baselines are absent but also the detailed comparisons are missing.

content.title: Persistence-based Contrastive Learning with Graph Neural Recurrent Networks for Time-series Forecasting
content.abstract: In the recent years, combinations of graph convolution and recurrent architectures have emerged as a new powerful alternative for multivariate spatio-temporal forecasting, with applications ranging from biosurveillance to traffic monitoring. However, such methods often tend to suffer from vulnerability to noise and limited generalization abilities, especially when semantics and structural properties of time series evolve over time. To address these limitations, we propose a simple yet flexible and highly effective framework, i.e., Persistence-based Contrastive Learning with Graph Neural Recurrent Networks (PCL-GCRN). The key idea behind PCL-GCRN is the notion of topological invariance that we introduce to contrastive graph learning for multivariate spatio-temporal processes. PCL-GCRN allows us to simultaneously focus on multiple most important data shape characteristics at different granularities that play the key role in the learning performance. As a result, PCL-GCRN leads to richer data augmentation, improved performance, and enhanced robustness. Our extensive experiments on a broad range of real-world datasets, from spatio-temporal forecasting of traffic to monkeypox surveillance, suggest that PCL-GCRN yields competitive results both in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness, outperforming 19 competing approaches.
